stem_md: A group of  $ 12 $  pirates agree to divide a treasure chest of gold coins among themselves as follows. The  $ k^\text{th} $  pirate to take a share takes  $ \frac{k}{12} $  of the coins that remain in the chest. The number of coins initially in the chest is the smallest number for which this arrangement will allow each pirate to receive a positive whole number of coins. How many coins does the  $ 12^{\text{th}} $  pirate receive? $ \textbf{(A)} \ 720 \qquad  \textbf{(B)} \ 1296 \qquad  \textbf{(C)} \ 1728 \qquad  \textbf{(D)} \ 1925 \qquad  \textbf{(E)} \ 3850 $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We work backwards.
Let there be  $c$  coins *before* the 12th pirate takes his share. Then, since the 11th pirate takes  $\frac{11}{12}^{\text{th}}$  of whatever he is given, he leaves  $\frac{1}{12}^{\text{th}}$  of it behind. So,  $c$  must be one twelfth of the amount before the 11th pirate. Hence, there were  $\frac{12}{1}c$  coins before the 11th pirate. Similarly, the 10th pirate takes  $\frac{10}{12}^{\text{th}}$  of what he receives and leaves behind  $\frac{2}{12}^{\text{th}}$  of it, so the number of coins before the 10th pirate would be  $\frac{12}{2}$  times the number of coins before the 11th pirate, which is  $\left(\frac{12}{1}\right)\left(\frac{12}{2}\right)c$ . Continuing this pattern, we get that in terms of  $c$ , the original number of coins must have been   $$ \left(\frac{12}{1}\right)\left(\frac{12}{2}\right)\left(\frac{12}{3}\right)\cdots\left(\frac{12}{11}\right)c. $$   Now we need to pick the smallest  $c$  such that this value is a positive integer. We can write it as   $$ \frac{12^{10}}{11!}c=\frac{2^{20} \cdot 3^{10}}{2^8 \cdot 3^4 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 5 \cdot 11}c=\frac{2^{12} \cdot 3^6}{5^2 \cdot 7 \cdot 11}c. $$   Then  $c$  must cancel the  $5^2 \cdot 7 \cdot 11$  such that this value is an integer. The smallest positive integer  $c$  that can do this is  $c=5^2 \cdot 7 \cdot 11$  itself, which is equal to  $\boxed{1925}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2013 Contests/2013 AMC 10/519729.json

Therefore, he takes 11!/12^11 of the pot, which upon prime factorization cancels out to 1925/2^14*3^8. Therefore, the least the twelfth pirate could have gotten is **(D) 1925**

stem_md: In a recent basketball game, Shenille attempted only three-point shots and two-point shots. She was successful on  $20\%$  of her three-point shots and  $30\%$  of her two-point shots. Shenille attempted  $30$  shots. How many points did she score? $ \textbf{(A)}\ 12\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 18\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 24\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 30\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 36 $
solution_md:
Let the number of attempted three-point shots made be  $x$  and the number of attempted two-point shots be  $y$ .  We know that  $x+y=30$ , and we need to evaluate  $(0.2\cdot3)x +(0.3\cdot2)y$ , as we know that the  three-point shots are worth 3 points and that she made 20% of them and that the two-point shots are worth 2 and that she made 30% of them.

Simplifying, we see that this is equal to  $0.6x + 0.6y = 0.6(x+y)$ .  Plugging in  $x+y=30$ , we get  $0.6(30) = \boxed{\textbf{(B) }18}$

stem_md: A student council must select a two-person welcoming committee and a three-person planning committee from among its members. There are exactly  $10$  ways to select a two-person team for the welcoming committee. It is possible for students to serve on both committees. In how many different ways can a three-person planning committee be selected? $ \textbf{(A)}\ 10\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 12\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 15\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 18\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 25$
solution_md:
Let  $n$  be the number of total members. Then we must have
\begin{align*}
&\binom{n}{2} = 10 
&\frac{n!}{2!(n - 2)!} = 10 
&\frac{n(n - 1)\cdot (n - 2)!}{2\cdot (n - 2)!} = 10 
&n(n - 1) = 20 
&n = 5.
\end{align*}
Then, the required answer is  $\binom{5}{3} = 10\text{ (A)}$

stem_md: Let points  $ A = (0,0) , \ B = (1,2), \ C = (3,3), $  and  $ D = (4,0) $ . Quadrilateral  $ ABCD $  is cut into equal area pieces by a line passing through  $ A $ . This line intersects  $ \overline{CD} $  at point  $ \left (\frac{p}{q}, \frac{r}{s} \right ) $ , where these fractions are in lowest terms. What is  $ p + q + r + s $ ? $ \textbf{(A)} \ 54 \qquad \textbf{(B)} \ 58 \qquad  \textbf{(C)} \ 62 \qquad \textbf{(D)} \ 70 \qquad \textbf{(E)} \ 75 $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>The total area of the quadrilateral is the sum of the areas of three triangles and the rectangle. So,  $\frac{(2)(1)}{2}+\frac{(2)(1)}{2}+\frac{(1)(3)}{2}+(2)(2)=\frac{15}{2}$ . Half of this area is  $\frac{15}{4}$ . Let the line passing through  $A$  and dividing the quadrilateral at point  $P$  be  $y=mx$ . Then, draw the line passing through  $P$  perpendicular to the x-axis, meeting the axis at  $Q$ . We know  $\overline{AQ}=x$  and  $
\overline{PQ}=mx$ Thus,  $[APQ]+[PQD]=\frac{15}{4}$ . 
Then,  $[APQ]+[PQD]=\frac{(mx)(x)}{2}+\frac{(4-x)(mx)}{2}=\frac{15}{4}$ . Thus,  $mx=\frac{15}{8}$ . 
We also know that the line connecting  $C$  and  $D$  can be represented by  $y=-3x+12$ . Thus  $mx=\frac{15}{8}=-3x+12$  -->  $x=\frac{27}{8}$  and  $P=(\frac{27}{8}, \frac{15}{8})$ .  $27+8+15+8=58$  -->  $\boxed{B}$</details>

Area of a triangle is  $\frac{1}{2} \cdot bh$  where  $b$  is the base of the triangle and  $h$  is the height.
In  $\triangle ABE$ ,  $$ 40=\frac{1}{2}*BE*10 $$    $$ \implies \frac{1}{2}BE=\frac{40}{10} $$    $$ \implies BE=4 \cdot 2=8 $$  Hence the answer is  $\boxed{(E)8}$ .

stem_md: A unit square is rotated  $45^\circ$  about its center. What is the area of the region swept out by the interior of the square? $ \textbf{(A)}\ 1-\frac{\sqrt2}2+\frac\pi4\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ \frac12+\frac\pi4\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 2-\sqrt2+\frac\pi4\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ \frac{\sqrt2}2+\frac\pi4\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 1+\frac{\sqrt2}4+\frac\pi8 $
solution_md:
Alternate formulation:  For a given angle of rotation  $\theta$  about the center, let  $S(\theta)$  represent the set of all points  $(x,y) \in \mathbb R^2$  interior to the square.  What is the area of the union of  $S(\theta)$  for all  $\theta \in [0, \pi/4]$ ?  Equivalently, what is the area of the set of all points  $(x,y)$  such that there exists some  $\theta \in [0,\pi/4]$  for which  $(x,y) \in S(\theta)$ ?

That would be the precise mathematical formulation (instead of saying "swept out"), but to be honest, "swept out" is just easier to say.

The answer is straightforward to calculate once the diagram is understood.  <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>For a square with side length 1, the distance from center to vertex is  $r = 1/\sqrt{2}$ , hence the area is composed of a semicircle of radius  $r$ , plus 4 times a parallelogram with height  $1/2$  and base  $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2(1+\sqrt{2})}$ .  That is to say, the total area is  $\frac{1}{2} \pi (1/\sqrt{2})^2 + 4 \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4(1+\sqrt{2})} = \frac{\pi}{4} + 2 - \sqrt{2}$ .</details>

Note that this if we write in polar the square as  $s(\theta)$ , the problem is really just asking for the  $\int_{0}^{2\pi} \max_{\theta\in [x,x+45^\circ]}s(\theta) x dx$ . In particular, we will observe and use the fact that  $\max_{\theta\in [x,x+45^\circ]}s(\theta)$  is equal to one of  $s(x),s(x+45^\circ), \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ .

We don't actually compute integrals. However, the observation implies that other than the starting and finishing unit squares, the only additional area is that every other  $\frac{\pi}{4}$  arc is also swept.

We may now compute the area as
\[4\left(\frac{1}{8}\cdot \pi (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})^2 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{2}\right)= \frac{\pi}{4}+2-\sqrt{2}= \textbf{(C)}\]

stem_md: Central High School is competing against Northern High School in a backgammon match. Each school has three players, and the contest rules require that each player play two games against each of the other's school's players. The match takes place in six rounds, with three games played simultaneously in each round. In how many different ways can the match be scheduled? $\textbf{(A)} \ 540 \qquad  \textbf{(B)} \ 600 \qquad  \textbf{(C)} \ 720 \qquad  \textbf{(D)} \ 810 \qquad  \textbf{(E)} \ 900$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Call the Central players  $A, B, C$  and call the Northern players  $1, 2, 3$ . Consider the  $6$  matches  $1$  plays. Then there are  $\binom{6}{2} \cdot \binom{4}{2} = 90$  possibilities to arrange  $AA, BB, CC$ . Then consider opponent  $2$ 's matches. Suppose that  $A$  plays  $2$  at the same time that  $B$  plays  $1$  both matches. Then there is only one possibility, and similarly for  $C$ . Now consider the possibility that  $A$  plays  $2$  while  $B$  plays  $1$  for one match, and  $A$  plays  $2$  while  $C$  plays  $1$  for the other match. Then there are  $4$  possibilities to arrange  $A$ , and  $2$  possibilities to choose who plays  $2$  first out of  $B$  and  $C$ . This results in  $2 + 4 \cdot 2 = 10$  total possibilities. Notice that  $C$ 's opponents are automatically decided by the matches that  $1$  and  $2$  play. Hence, there are a total of  $90 \cdot 10 = \boxed{900}$  possibilities.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2013 Contests/2013 AMC 10/519774.json

So it's basically permuting abcabc, for which there are  $\frac{6!}{2!2!2!}$  orderings, which is 90. Thus the answer must be divisible by 90 and we can eliminate choice B.

How many three-digit numbers are not divisible by  $5$ , have digits that sum to less than  $20$ , and have the first digit equal to the third digit? $\textbf{(A) }52\qquad
\textbf{(B) }60\qquad
\textbf{(C) }66\qquad
\textbf{(D) }68\qquad
\textbf{(E) }70\qquad$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We see that our number must be of the form  $\overline{aba}$  where  $a\not=5$  and  $2a+b<20$ .

We see that when  $1\le a\le4$ , there are  $10$  values of  $b$ , so that is  $4\cdot10=40$  in total.

We see that when  $6\le a\le9$ , there are  $20-2a$  values of  $b$ , so that is  $(8+2)2=20$  in total.

We get the final answer of  $40+20=\boxed{60}$ .</details>

Two sides of a triangle have lengths  $10$  and  $15$ .  The length of the altitude to the third side is the average of the lengths of the altitudes to the two given sides.  How long is the third side? $\textbf{(A) }6\qquad
\textbf{(B) }8\qquad
\textbf{(C) }9\qquad
\textbf{(D) }12\qquad
\textbf{(E) }18\qquad$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Trolling</summary>The side should have a length between  $10$  and  $15$  to make the area stay the same.  $\boxed{(\text D)\ 12}$  is the only answer choice that satisfies this.</details>

<details><summary>Actual Solution</summary>Let the altitudes to the sides that have length  $10$  and  $15$  have length  $a$  and  $b$ , respectively. 
We have  $10a=15b$  because the area is constant, thus  $a=\frac32b$ . 
If we let  $x$  be the length of the missing side, and  $c$  be the length of the altitude to it, then we also have  $cx=15b$ .  $c=\frac{a+b}2$ , so  $15b=x\cdot\frac{b+\frac32b}2\Rightarrow \boxed{x=12}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2013 Contests/2013 AMC 10/519786.json

<details><summary>Note</summary>This is the harmonic mean of  $10$  and  $15$ , or  $\boxed{12}$ . This is easy to show by writing each height as  $\frac{2A}{b}$ , where  $A$  denotes the area of the triangle and  $b$  is the base to which the height is extended to.</details>

A triangle with vertices  $(6,5)$ ,  $(8,-3)$ , and  $(9,1)$  is reflected about the line  $x=8$  to create a second triangle.  What is the area of the union of the two triangles? $\textbf{(A) }9\qquad
\textbf{(B) }\dfrac{28}{3}\qquad
\textbf{(C) }10\qquad
\textbf{(D) }\dfrac{31}{3}\qquad
\textbf{(E) }\dfrac{32}{3}\qquad$
solution_md:
The 4 points we have are  $(6,5), (8,-3), (10,5),$  and  $(8, \frac{7}{3})$  (as KingSmasher3 originally noted).  

We line them up in clockwise order:  $(8,-3), (6,5), (8, \frac{7}{3}), (10,5)$ . 

Then the area is
\[\frac{1}{2}|(8\cdot 5 + 6\cdot \frac{7}{3} + 8 \cdot 5 + 10\cdot -3) - (-3\cdot 6 + 5\cdot 8 + \frac{7}{3}\cdot 10 + 5\cdot 8).|\]
Simplifying gives
\[\frac{1}{2}|64 - \frac{256}{3}| = \frac{1}{2}|\frac{192}{3} - \frac{256}{3}| = \frac{1}{2}|\frac{64}{3}| = \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{64}{3} = \boxed{\frac{32}{3}}. \blacksquare \]

stem_md:
Daphne is visited periodically by her three best friends: Alice, Beatrix, and Claire.  Alice visits every third day, Beatrix visits every fourth day, and Claire visits every fifth day.  All three friends visited Daphne yesterday.  How many days of the next  $365$ -day period will exactly two friends visit her? $\textbf{(A) }48\qquad
\textbf{(B) }54\qquad
\textbf{(C) }60\qquad
\textbf{(D) }66\qquad
\textbf{(E) }72\qquad$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Here, we must find LCMs.  The LCM of  $3$  and  $4$  is 12, so Alice and Beatrix both visit every twelve days.  The LCM of  $3$  and  $5$  is  $15$ , so Alice and Claire both visit every fifteen days.  The LCM of  $4$  and  $5$  is  $20$ , so Beatrix and Claire both visit every twenty days.  All three visit every sixty days, so we are counting numbers that are less than or equal to 365, and are multiples of  $12$ ,  $15$ , or  $20$ , but not  $60$ .  There are  $30$  multiples of  $12$ ,  $24$  multiples of 15, and  $18$  multiples of 20  $\le 365$ .  There are  $6$  multiples of  $60$ .  We counted them three times and want them zero times, so we must subtract them  $3$  times.  Therefore, the answer is  $30+24+18-3(6)=\boxed{(B) 54}$ .</details>

In base  $10$ , the number  $2013$  ends in the digit  $3$ .  In base  $9$ , on the other hand, the same number is written as  $(2676)_9$  and ends in the digit  $6$ .  For how many positive integers  $b$  does the base- $b$  representation of  $2013$  end in the digit  $3$ ? $\textbf{(A) }6\qquad
\textbf{(B) }9\qquad
\textbf{(C) }13\qquad
\textbf{(D) }16\qquad
\textbf{(E) }18\qquad$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>In base  $b$ , the units digit is 3 iff  $b>3$  and  $2013\equiv 3\pmod{b}\implies2010\equiv0\pmod{b}$ . Since  $2010=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot67$ , 2010 has 16 divisors,  $\boxed{13}$  of which is greater than 3.</details>

stem_md: In triangle  $ABC$ ,  $AB=13$ ,  $BC=14$ , and  $CA=15$ . Distinct points  $D$ ,  $E$ , and  $F$  lie on segments  $\overline{BC}$ ,  $\overline{CA}$ , and  $\overline{DE}$ , respectively, such that  $\overline{AD}\perp\overline{BC}$ ,  $\overline{DE}\perp\overline{AC}$ , and  $\overline{AF}\perp\overline{BF}$ . The length of segment  $\overline{DF}$  can be written as  $\frac{m}{n}$ , where  $m$  and  $n$  are relatively prime positive integers. What is  $m+n$ ? ${ \textbf{(A)}\ 18\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 21\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 24\qquad\textbf{(D}}\ 27\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 30 $

This was a nice problem :)
SolutionSince $\angle{AFB}=\angle{ADB}=90$ , quadrilateral $ABDF$ is cyclic. It follows that $\angle{ADE}=\angle{ABF}$ . In addition, since $\angle{AFB}=\angle{AED}=90$ , triangles $ABF$ and $ADE$ are similar. It follows that $AF=(13)(\frac{4}{5}), BF=(13)(\frac{3}{5})$ . By Ptolemy, we have $13DF+(5)(13)(\frac{4}{5})=(12)(13)(\frac{3}{5})$ . Cancelling $13$ , the rest is easy. We obtain $DF=\frac{16}{5}\implies{16+5=21}\implies{\boxed{(B)}}$

This means $\frac{4x}{15-3x}=\frac{3x-63}{4x-20}$ , so $x=\frac{189}{25} \implies F = \left(\frac{189}{25}, \frac{48}{25}\right)$ . Distance formula gives a distance of $\frac{16}{5} \implies \boxed{\text{(B)}}$ .

I'm not sure what proof Evan had in mind in the spring of 2013. He started writing his geometry book in the fall of the same year, and while he writes this exact fact in the first chapter of his book, I don't see any proof mentioned. I couldn't find anything online either. While the fact is mentioned on Wikipedia and references one of Titu's books, I couldn't find a proof in that book either. So, here's my own argument.**Fact.** A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic if and only if $\angle ABD = \angle ACD$ . [asy] import olympiad; pair A,B,C,D; A=(0.1,0.6); B=(0,0); C=(0.94,0); D=(0.7,0.7); dot(A); dot(B); dot(C); dot(D); draw(A--B--C--D--cycle); draw(A--C); draw(B--D); draw(circumcircle(A,B,C)); label(" $A$ ",A,NW); label(" $B$ ",B,SW); label(" $C$ ",C,SE); label(" $D$ ",D,NE); [/asy] *Proof.* We start with the easy direction. Assume quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic. Then $\angle ABD$ and $\angle ACD$ are inscribed angles that both intercept arc $AD$ . By the inscribed angle theorem, these angles both have measure equal to half the measure of arc $AD$ . Thus they are equal. [asy] import olympiad; pair A,B,C,D; A=(0.1,0.6); B=(0,0); C=(0.94,0); D=(0.7,0.7); dot(A); dot(B); dot(C); dot(D); draw(A--B--C--D--cycle); draw(A--C); draw(B--D); draw(circumcircle(A,B,C),invisible); markscalefactor=0.02; draw(anglemark(D,B,A)); draw(anglemark(D,C,A)); label(" $A$ ",A,NW); label(" $B$ ",B,SW); label(" $C$ ",C,SE); label(" $D$ ",D,NE); [/asy] The other direction takes more detail. Assume $\angle ABD = \angle ACD$ . It is known that three points determine a circle. Take the circle containing points $A$ , $C$ , and $D$ . We will finish by showing $B$ also lies on this circle. By the inscribed angle theorem, we again have $\angle ACD$ has measure equal to half the measure of arc $AD$ . Say $B$ lies inside the circle. By a corollary of the inscribed angle theorem, we have that $\angle ABD$ is half the sum of the measures of the two arcs intercepted by $\angle ABD$ and its vertical angle, namely arc $AD$ and some other arc of positive measure. But given the assumed equality, we find the other arc must have a zero measure, which is a contradiction. Say $B$ lies outside the circle. By a corollary of the inscribed angle theorem, we have that $\angle ABD$ is half the difference of the measures of the two arcs intercepted by $\angle ABD$ , namely arc $AD$ and some other arc of positive measure. But given the assumed equality, we find the other arc must have a zero measure, which is a contradiction. So $B$ must be on the circle, and we are done. $\Box$

Let  $\omega$  be the circle with diameter  $AB$ . Clearly  $F = \omega\cap DE$ . We now use coordinates with  $D = (0,0)$ ,  $A = (0, 12)$ ,  $B = (-5, 0)$ , and  $C = (9, 0)$ . Line  $AC$  has slope  $-4/3$ , so  $DE$  has slope  $3/4$ , and since it passes through the origin, its equation is  $y = 3x/4$ . Also,  $\omega$  has center  $(-5/2, 6)$  and radius  $13/2$ , so its equation is  $(x  + 5/2)^2 + (y- 6)^2 = 169/4$ . 

We now find the intersections of the line  $DE$  and the circle  $\omega$  by plugging  $y= 3x/4$  into the circle equation:
\[ (x + 5/2)^2 + (3x/4 - 6)^2 = 169/4\implies \frac{25}{16}x^2 - 4x + \frac{169}{4} =\frac{169}{4}\implies x\in \{0, 64/25\}.\]
Note that  $x = 0$  just gives the point  $D$ , so we focus on  $x = 64/25$ . Then,  $y = \frac{3}{4}x = 48/25$ , so  $F = (64/25, 48/25)$ . Finally,
\[ DF = \sqrt{(64/25)^2 + (48/25)^2} = \frac{16}{25}\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \frac{16}{5}.\]

We first use Heron's Formula on  $\triangle ABC$  to get  $[ABC] = 84,$  which implies that  $AD = 12.$  Therefore,  $\triangle ABD$  is a  $5-12-13$  right triangle and  $ADC$  is a  $9-12-15$  right triangle. Since  $\angle AFB = \angle ADB = 90^{\circ},$   $ABCD$  is a cyclic quadrilateral. stem_md: Bernardo chooses a three-digit positive integer  $N$  and writes both its base-5 and base-6 representations on a blackboard. Later LeRoy sees the two numbers Bernardo has written. Treating the two numbers as base-10 integers, he adds them to obtain an integer  $S$ . For example, if  $N=749$ , Bernardo writes the numbers 10,444 and 3,245, and LeRoy obtains the sum  $S=13,689$ . For how many choices of  $N$  are the two rightmost digits of  $S$ , in order, the same as those of  $2N$ ? ${ \textbf{(A)}\ 5\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 10\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 15\qquad\textbf{(D}}\ 20\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 25 $
solution_md:
To compare the last two digits, the main strategy is to look at the  $\textit{units}$  and  $\textit{tens}$  digit  $\textbf{separately}$  $\textbf{Units}$  digit:
Let the base  $5$  and  $6$  representations of  $N$  end with  $a$  and  $b$  respectively. The units digit of  $S$  is thus  $a + b \pmod{10}$ Comparing the units digit of  $2N$  and  $S$ , we find:
\[2N \equiv S \pmod{10} \Rightarrow 2a \equiv a + b \pmod{10}\]

This implies,  $\Rightarrow a \equiv b \pmod{10}$ . And since  $a \in [0, 4]$  ( $a$  is base  $5$  digit) and  $b \in [0, 5]$  ( $b$  is base  $6$  digit), we must have  $a = b \in [0, 4]$ . So,
\begin{align}
    N \equiv a \pmod{5}
    N \equiv b \equiv a  \pmod{6}
\end{align} $N$  is  $a$  more than a multiple  $5$  and also  $a$  more than a multiple  $6$  meaning  $N$  is  $a$  more than a multiple of  $\text{lcm}(5, 6) = 30$ This is very nice because the units digit will  $\texttt{not}$  carry when adding as  $a + a  = 2a \le 2 \cdot 4 = 8$   $$ N \equiv a \pmod{30} \quad\text{where } 0 \le a \le 4 $$   $\textbf{Tens}$  digit:
Let  $N = 30k + a$  where  $4 \le k \le 33$  ( $N$  must be  $3$ -digit)
Now as  $a$  won't affect the tens digit by carrying (by the bounds of  $0 \le a \le 4$ ), for each valid  $k$ , there will be  $a = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 \Rightarrow 5$  values of  $N$  too satisfy the condition.

The tens digit of  $N$  base  $5$  representation is  $\frac{30k}{5} \equiv 6k \equiv k \pmod{5}$ You may ask  $\texttt{Why?}$ Consider   $$ A = \overline{d_n d_{n-1}\cdots d_1 d_0}_b = d_n \cdot b^n + d_{n-1} \cdot b^{n-1} + \cdots + d_1 \cdot b + d_ 0 $$  If we remove the units digit (remove units digit  $a$  in  $N = 30k + a$ ), what is left is  $$ \overline{d_n d_{n-1}\cdots d_1}_b = d_n \cdot b^n + d_{n-1} \cdot b^{n-1} + \cdots + d_1 \cdot b $$  In which the tens digit  $d_1$  can be determined by  $\div b$  and taking the remainder. 
Similarly the tens digit of  $N$  base  $6$  representation is  $\frac{30k}{6} \equiv 5k \pmod{6}$ The tens digit of  $2N$  is simply  $2 \cdot 3 k = 6k \pmod{10}$ Let  $\%$  denote the remainder.  $$ k\%5 + 5k\%6 \equiv 6k \pmod{10} $$  Let  $k\%5 = r$  ie  $k \equiv r \pmod{5}$  equivalently,  $k = r + 5m$  where  $0 \le r \le 4$ . The equation becomes  $$ r + [5(r + 5m)\%6] \equiv 6(r + 5m) \pmod{10} $$    $$ (5r + m) \%6 \equiv 5r \pmod{10} $$    $$ 5r + m \equiv 5r\%10 \pmod{6}  $$    $$ m \equiv (5r\%10) - r \pmod{6} $$   $\texttt{Case }  r = 0$ :  $\rightarrow m \equiv 0 \pmod{6} \Rightarrow k \equiv 0 \pmod{30}$  $\texttt{Case }  r = 1$ :  $\rightarrow m \equiv 0 \pmod{6} \Rightarrow k \equiv 1 \pmod{30}$  $\texttt{Case }  r = 2: $  $\rightarrow m \equiv 2 \pmod{6} \Rightarrow k \equiv 12 \pmod{30}$  $\texttt{Case }  r = 3$ :  $\rightarrow m \equiv 2 \pmod{6} \Rightarrow k \equiv 13 \pmod{30}$  $\texttt{Case }  r = 4$ :  $\rightarrow m \equiv 4 \pmod{6} \Rightarrow k \equiv 24 \pmod{30}$ For  $r = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$  each have  $1$  value of  $k \in [4, 33]$ , and there are  $5$  valid  $a$ , and for each  $k$  we have thus the answer is  $5 \cdot 5 = \boxed{25}$ Side Note: To solve nested or multiple remainders, it is often a good idea to create a variable for the remainder, then substitute

Then the last 2 digits (base 5) are 20, so the last 2 digits (base 6) are 00. So it is congruent to 0 (mod 36). Since  $60 \equiv 0 (mod 4)$ , we get a solution in this case.**Case 8:  $N$  ends in 70**
Then the last 2 digits (base 5) are 40, so the last 2 digits (base 6) are 00. So it is congruent to 0 (mod 36). Since  $70 \not\equiv 0 (mod 4)$ , we get no solution in this case.**Case 9:  $N$  ends in 80**
Then the last 2 digits (base 5) are 10, so the last 2 digits (base 6) are 50. So it is congruent to 30 (mod 36). Since  $80 \not\equiv 30 (mod 4)$ , we get no solution in this case.**Case 10:  $N$  ends in 90**
Then the last 2 digits (base 5) are 30, so the last 2 digits (base 6) are 50. So it is congruent to 30 (mod 36). Since  $90 \equiv 30 (mod 4)$ , we get a solution in this case.

stem_md: The real numbers  $c, b, a$  form an arithmetic sequence with  $a\ge b\ge c\ge 0$ . The quadratic  $ax^2+bx+c$  has exactly one root. What is this root? $\textbf{(A)}\ -7-4\sqrt{3}\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ -2-\sqrt{3}\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ -1\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ -2+\sqrt{3}\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ -7+4\sqrt{3} $
solution_md:
My favorite problem on the AMC10B :D
<details><summary>neat but a bit long</summary>It is given that  $ax^2+bx+c=0$  has 1 real root, so the discriminant is zero, or  $b^2=4ac$ . Because a, b, c are in arithmetic progression,  $b-a=c-b$ , or  $b=\frac {a+c} {2} $ . We need to find the unique root, or  $-\frac {b} {2a} $  (discriminant is 0). From  $b^2=4ac$ , we have  $-\frac {b} {2a} =-\frac {2c} {b}$ . Ignoring the negatives, we have  $\frac {2c} {b} = \frac {2c} {\frac {a+c} {2}} = \frac {4c} {a+c} = \frac {1} {\frac {1} {\frac {4c} {a+c}}} = \frac {1} {\frac {a+c} {4c}} = \frac {1} {\frac {a} {4c} + \frac {1} {4} }$ . Fortunately, finding  $\frac {a} {c} $  is not very hard. Plug in  $b=\frac {a+c} {2}$  to  $b^2=4ac$ , we have  $a^2+2ac+c^2=16ac$ , or  $a^2-14ac+c^2=0$ , and dividing by  $c^2$  gives  $(\frac {a} {c} ) ^2-14( \frac {a} {c} ) +1 = 0$ , so  $\frac {a} {c} = \frac {14 \pm \sqrt {192} } {2} = 7 \pm 4 \sqrt {3} $ . But  $7-4\sqrt {3} <1$ , violating the assumption that  $a \ge c$ . Therefore,  $\frac {a} {c} = 7 +4\sqrt {3} $ . Plugging this in, we have  $\frac {1} {\frac {a} {4c} + \frac {1} {4} } = \frac {1} {2+ \sqrt {3} } = 2- \sqrt {3} $ . But we need the negative of this, so the answer is  $\boxed {D}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>If the quadratic has one root, then it must be  $-\dfrac{b}{2a},$  the vertex of the parabola. Then we also have  $b^2-4ac = 0,$  or  $b^2 = 4ac.$  Because  $c, b, a$  is an arithmetic sequence,  $b = \dfrac{1}{2} (a+c),$  so we can write the root as  $-\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}(a+c)}{2a} = -\dfrac{1}{4}(1+\dfrac{c}{a}).$  Thus, we must find  $\dfrac{c}{a}.$   $b^2 = 4ac$  and  $b = \dfrac{1}{2}(a+c),$  so  $\dfrac{1}{4}(a+c)^2 = 4ac.$  This simplifies to  $a^2 - 14ac + c^2 = 0.$  Because  $a\neq 0,$  we can divide by  $a^2$  to get  $\dfrac{c^2}{a^2} - 14\dfrac{c}{a} + 1 = 0.$  We now have a quadratic in  $\dfrac{c}{a}$ :  $\left(\dfrac{c}{a}\right)^2 - 14\dfrac{c}{a} + 1 = 0.$  Using the quadratic formula, \[\dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{14\pm8\sqrt{3}}{2} = 7 \pm 4\sqrt{3}.\] Because  $c\le a$ , we must take the choice that is less than  $1$ , so  $\dfrac{c}{a} = 7 - 4\sqrt{3},$  and thus the root is  $-\dfrac{1}{4}(8-4\sqrt{3}) = -2+\sqrt{3}.$  The answer is  $\boxed{\textbf{D}}$ .</details>

stem_md: The number  $2013$  has the property that its units digit is the sum of its other digits, that is  $2+0+1=3$ . How many integers less than  $2013$  but greater than  $1000$  share this property? ${ \textbf{(A)}\ 33 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 34 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 45 \qquad\textbf{(D)}}\ 46\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 58 $
solution_md:
We can split this into two cases:

Case 1:  $1000\leq abcd \leq 1999$ Our number has the form  $1bcd$  where  $d=b+c+1$ . Since  $d$  is a digit then  $d\leq9 \rightarrow 0\leq b+c\leq8$ . For any pair of nonnegative b and c, d is determined. So we want to count the number of pairs (b,c). The number of pairs for  $ b+c\leq8$  is the same as the number of pairs for  $b+c+x=8$  where x is nonnegative. This has  $\binom{10}{2}=45$  solutions. 

Case 2:  $2000\leq abcd \leq 2012$ It is easy enough to check that only  $2002$  works.

Therefore the total is  $45+1=\boxed {46} \rightarrow \boxed {D}$

stem_md: Two non-decreasing sequences of nonnegative integers have different first terms. Each sequence has the property that each term beginning with the third is the sum of the previous two terms, and the seventh term of each sequence is  $N$ . What is the smallest possible value of  $N$ ? ${ \textbf{(A)}\ 55\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 89\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 104\qquad\textbf{(D}}\ 144\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 273 $
solution_md:
Let the two sequences be 
\[
a, b, a + b, a + 2b, 2a + 3b, 3a + 5b, 5a + 8b, \cdots
c, d, c + d, c + 2d, 2c + 3d, 3c + 5d, 5c + 8d, \cdots
\]
Where  $a \le b$ ,  $c \le d$ . Wlog  $a > c \ge 0$ , as simply swapping the variable names becomes the other case
The  $7^\text{th}$  term,  $N = 5a + 8b = 5c + 8d$   $$ 5(a - c) = 8(d - b) $$  For some positive integer  $k$ ,
\[
\begin{cases}
a - c = 8k
d - b = 5k
\end{cases}
\]
This implies  $a > c$  and  $d > b$ . And because  $b \ge a$  (non-decreasing sequences), results in the inequality   $$ d > b \ge a > c \ge 0 $$   $a = c + 8k$  and  $d = b + 5k$ , substituting this in the inequality we have  $$ b + 5k > b \ge c + 8k > c \ge 0  $$  To minimize, set the variables to minimum value  $k = 1$  and  $c = 0$ . It follows that  $13 > 8 \ge 8 > 0$  
The answer is thus  $8 \cdot 13 = \boxed{104}$

We are given that the seventh terms of both sequences are equal, so  $5a+8b=5c+8d \Longrightarrow 5(a-c)=8(d-b)$ . stem_md: Alex has  $75$  red tokens and  $75$  blue tokens. There is a booth where Alex can give two red tokens and receive in return a silver token and a blue token, and another booth where Alex can give three blue tokens and receive in return a silver token and a red token. Alex continues to exchange tokens until no more exchanges are possible. How many silver tokens will Alex have at the end? ${ \textbf{(A)}\ 62 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 82 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 83\qquad\textbf{(D}}\ 102\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 103 $
solution_md:
Well, the "bashing"is generally easy. Here's what you do:

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>First, you take out all blue tokens: $0$  blue,  $100$  red, and  $25$  silver.

Then, we divide  $100$  by  $2$  to get no red coins, get  $50$  blue coins and  $75$  silver.

For our third step, we divide  $50$  by  $3$  to get  $16$ , with  $2$  blue coins left over. Now, we get  $2$  blue coins,  $16$  red coins, and  $91$  silver coins. 

Next, we divide  $16$  by  $2$ , to get  $0$  red coins,  $99$  silver coins, and  $10$  blue coins. 

Now, we divide the blue coins by  $3$ , yielding  $3$  red coins,  $102$  silver coins, and  $1$  blue coin. 

We can't forget that  $2$  will still go into  $3$  once, so:

We have  $1$  red coin,  $103$  silver coins, and we have  $2$  blue coins, therefore we are done. 



The answer is  $\boxed{103}$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2013 Contests/2013 AMC 10/521747.json

stem_md: A wire is cut into two pieces, one of length  $a$  and the other of length  $b$ . The piece of length  $a$  is bent to form an equilateral triangle, and the piece of length  $b$  is bent to form a regular hexagon. The triangle and the hexagon have equal area. What is  $\frac{a}{b}$ ? ${ \textbf{(A)}\ 1 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} \qquad\textbf{(C)}\ \sqrt{3}\qquad\textbf{(D}}\ 2 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\ \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} $
solution_md:
The answer is (B).
Using the formulas for area of a regular triangle  $(\frac{{s}^{2}\sqrt{3}}{4})$  and regular hexagon  $(\frac{3{s}^{2}\sqrt{3}}{2})$  and plugging  $\frac{a}{3}$  and  $\frac{b}{6}$  into each equation, you find that  $\frac{{a}^{2}\sqrt{3}}{36}=\frac{{b}^{2}\sqrt{3}}{24}$ . Simplifying this, you get  $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}$ .

stem_md: Define  $a\clubsuit b=a^2b-ab^2$ . Which of the following describes the set of points  $(x, y)$  for which  $x\clubsuit y=y\clubsuit x$ ? ${ \textbf{(A)}\ \text{a finite set of points}  \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ \text{one line}  \qquad\textbf{(C)}\  \text{two parallel lines} \qquad\textbf{(D}}\  \text{two intersecting lines} \qquad\textbf{(E)}\  \text{three lines} $
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>We have  $x^2y-y^2x=y^2x-x^2y \Longrightarrow x^2y=y^2x$ . When  $x,y \ne 0$ , we can divide by  $xy$  to get  $y=x$ . However, when  $x=0$  or  $y=0$ , our original equation still holds. Thus, the solutions are the lines  $y=x$ ,  $x=0$ , and  $y=0$ , which are three distinct lines.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2013 Contests/2013 AMC 10/521753.json

Therefore, either  $xy=0$ , in which case the solution is the x-axis and y-axis, or  $x-y=0$ , in which case the solution is the line  $y=x$ . Therefore, the set of points is in the form of three lines.

<details><summary>Full Solution</summary>We start with a equation of course: $a^2b-ab^2=b^2a-ba^2$ Thus,  $2a^2b=2ab^2$ We now need casework:
Case 1:  $ab$  is not equal to 0.
Dividing by ab gives a=b, so we have part of a line: x=y other than (0, 0).
Case 2:  $ab=0$ .
Then either a=0 or b=0, or both. Trying a=0 or b=0 gives 0=0, so we have x=0 and y=0.

Since (0, 0) is part of x=0, we have E) three lines.</details>

xy(x-y)&=&0

solution_md:
In $\triangle ABC$ , medians $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{CE}$ intersect at $P$ , $PE=1.5$ , $PD=2$ , and $DE=2.5$ . What is the area of $AEDC?$ [asy] unitsize(75); draw((0,0)--(2,0)--(1/2,1)--cycle); draw((0,0)--(1.25,0.5)); draw((1/2,1)--(1,0)); draw((1,0)--(1.25,0.5)); label("P", (5/6, 1/3), NE); label("A", (0,0), SW); label("E", (1,0), S); label("B", (2,0), E); label("D", (1.25, 0.5), NE); label("C", (1/2, 1), N); [/asy] $\textbf{(A)}\ 13 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 13.5 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 14 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 14.5 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 15 $
Fastest Solution So Far$[ACDE] = \dfrac{CE \cdot AD}{2} = \dfrac{(1.5 \cdot 3)(2 \cdot 3)}{2} = \boxed{13.5}$
ExplanationIt is well known that the area of a quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals is half the product of the diagonals. This is because $[ACDE] = \dfrac{CE \cdot AP}{2} + \dfrac{CE \cdot PD}{2} = \dfrac{CE}{2} (AP + PD) = \dfrac{CE \cdot AD}{2}$ . Also, it is well known that the centroid splits medians in a $2:1$ ratio.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2013 Contests/2013 AMC 10/521757.json

candidates: Notice that  $\triangle PED$  is a 3-4-5 triangle with right angle at  $P$ . Then, using the property that the centroid divides the medians into lengths of ratio 2:1,  $PA=4$  and  $PC=3$ . Now that you have the base and height measurements for all four right triangles in  $AEDC$ , you can add their areas: 6+3+3+1.5 = 13.5 (B).

<details><summary>Another Way</summary>Notice that  $DPE$  is a right triangle
<details><summary>Proof</summary>$DP^2 + PE^2 = DE^2$  $ \Rightarrow 2^2 + 1.5^2 = 2.5^2$  $\Rightarrow 4 + 2.25 = 6.25$  $\Rightarrow 6.25 = 6.25$  :)</details>

Therefore  $CPA$  is a right angle.
Also since  $DE$  is parallel to  $CA$ <details><summary>Proof of this</summary>Median of triangle is parallel to the side which the median doesn't touch</details>

we can see that  $\triangle DPE$  is similar to  $\triangle CPA$ <details><summary>Proof of this</summary>DE is parallel to CA, alt. interior angles, etc</details>

So, by setting up a proportion  we get $CP = 3$  and  $PA = 4$ Also  $CA  = 5$ <details><summary>Why?</summary>Median  $DE$  is half as long as  $AC$  (geometry theorem)
Therefore  $AC = 2*DE \Rightarrow 5$</details>

Now we can find the area's of triangles  $CPA, CPD, DPE$ , and  $APE$  $\Rightarrow 3 + 6 + 3 + 1.5$  $\Rightarrow 13.5$ WHEW!</details>

<details><summary>A Little Quicker</summary>First note that AD is perpendicular to CE.
Ways to do this:
1) Assume this.  This is what I did on the test.  NOT RECOMMENDED, I just got lucky.
2) 1.5^2+2^2=2.5^2
3) (What I did after the test)  Because centroid divides medians into 2:1, CP=3 and AP=4.  Thus PAC is similar to PDE by SAS with a scale factor of 2; thus, AC=5 and you have the more obvious 3-4-5 right triangle.

To finish, use only two triangles: either CAD and ADE or ACE and CDE.  
CAD/ADE: Note that CP is the altitude of CAD=3, so the area of CAD is (1/2)(AD)(3).  Similarly, PE is the altitude of ADE=1.5, so the area of ADE is (1/2)(AD)(1.5).  Since AD=6, the total area is (1/2)(6)(3+1.5)=3(4.5)=B) 13.5
ACE/CDE is similar, with AP and PD as the altitudes and CE as the common base.  We get (1/2)(4.5)(2+4) which is also 13.5.</details>

Here is a solution to this elegant problem: We evaluate the general value $$ S_n=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n 2i}{\sum_{i=1}^n 2i-1}-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n 2i-1}{\sum_{i=1}^n 2i}. $$ In order to do so, we prove a few preliminary claims.**Claim 1:** $\sum_{i=1}^n 2i=n(n+1).$ *Proof.* Notice $$ \sum_{i=1}^n 2i=2\sum_{i=1}^n i, $$ so it suffices to prove $\sum_{i=1}^n i=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}.$ We proceed by induction, letting $f(n)=\sum_{i=1}^n i.$ For the base case $n=1,$ clearly, $f(1)=\frac{1(2)}{2}=1.$ Assume $f(k)=\frac{k(k+1)}{2},$ and note $$ f(k+1)=f(k)+(k+1)=\frac{k(k+1)}{2}+(k+1)=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}. $$ Our inductive step is complete and our result follows. $\blacksquare$ **Claim 2:** $\sum_{i=1}^n 2i-1=n^2.$ *Proof.* Notice $$ \sum_{i=1}^n 2i-1=\sum_{i=1}^n 2i-\sum_{i=1}^n 1=2\sum_{i=1}^n i-n. $$ Hence, by Claim 1, we see $$ \sum_{i=1}^n 2i-1=2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}-n=n(n+1)-n=n^2. $$ We are done. $\blacksquare$ We are now ready to approach $S_n.$ First, we let $a=\sum_{i=1}^n 2i$ and $b=\sum_{i=1}^n 2i-1,$ and observe $$ S_n=\frac{a}{b}-\frac{b}{a}=\frac{a^2-b^2}{ab}=\frac{(a-b)(a+b)}{ab}. $$ Substituting using our claims yields $$ S_n=\frac{[n(n+1)+n^2][n(n+1)-n^2]}{[n(n+1)][n^2]}=\frac{(2n^2+n)(n)}{(n^2)(n^2+n)}=\frac{2n+1}{n^2+n}. $$ Plugging in $n=3,$ we have $S_3=\frac{2\cdot 3+1}{3^2+3}=\frac{7}{12}.$ Our answer is $C.$

stem_md: Ray's car averages 40 miles per gallon of gasoline, and Tom's car averages 10 miles per gallon of gasoline. Ray and Tom each drive the same number of miles. What is the cars' combined rate of miles per gallon of gasoline? $ \textbf{(A) }10\qquad\textbf{(B) }16\qquad\textbf{(C) }25\qquad\textbf{(D) }30\qquad\textbf{(E) }40 $
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution 2</summary>Set the number of miles each drove to  $x$ . Then, the number of gallons Ray used would be  $\dfrac{x}{40}$  and for Tom would be  $\dfrac{x}{10} = \dfrac{4x}{40}$ . In total, they drove  $2x$  miles. stem_md: Real numbers  $x$  and  $y$  satisfy the equation  $x^2+y^2=10x-6y-34$ . What is  $x+y$ ? $ \textbf{(A) }1\qquad\textbf{(B) }2\qquad\textbf{(C) }3\qquad\textbf{(D) }6\qquad\textbf{(E) }8 $
solution_md:
<details><summary>SOL</summary>$x^2 + y^2 = 10x - 6y - 34$  $x^2 - 10x + y^2 + 6y = -34$  $(x-5)^2 -25  + (y+3)^2 - 9 = -34$ Bringing the  $-25$  and  $-9$  to the other side: $(x-5)^2 + (y+3)^2 = 0$ So the stuff inside the () is = 0.

Therefore: $x = 5, y = -3 \Rightarrow 5+(-3) = \boxed{2}$</details>

For example, if  $J=1$ , then  $2,9$  pair,  $3,8$  pair,  $4,7$  pair, etc. Thus, we can narrow it down to the ways to order these lines. Consider their individual orders. There are 4 choices for which line has  $A$ , 3 for  $B$ , 2 for  $C$ , and 1 for  $D$ . Thus, there are  $4!$  ways to arrange the lines. Each line can be flipped, for  $2^4$  additional combinations. So, the answer is  $3\cdot 4!\cdot 2^4=48\cdot 24$ . At this point, observe the units digit is  $2\implies \boxed{\text{C}}$</details>

<details><summary>solution</summary>There are three ways to chose the number  $j,$  which are  $1,$   $5,$  and  $9.$  Moreover, there are  $24$  ways to chose which pair of numbers go in which points no matter what the value of  $j$  is; there are no symmetries since the vertices are distinct. For each pair of vertices, there are  $2$  orientations (eg. 1,9 and 9,1). Since there are  $4$  pairs of vertices, there are  $2^4$  ways we can do that. Therefore, the number of distinct ways the octagon can be aissgned numbers is  $3*24*16 = \boxed{1152}$  or  $\boxed{\text{C}}.$</details>

The regular octagon $ABCDEFGH$ has its center at $J$ . Each of the vertices and the center are to be associated with one of the digits $1$ through $9$ , with each digit used once, in such a way that the sums of the numbers on the lines $AJE$ , $BJF$ , $CJG$ , and $DJH$ are all equal. In how many ways can this be done? $\textbf{(A)}\ 384 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 576 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 1152 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 1680 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 3456$ [asy] pair A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,J; A=(20,20(2+sqrt(2))); B=(20(1+sqrt(2)),20(2+sqrt(2))); C=(20(2+sqrt(2)),20(1+sqrt(2))); D=(20(2+sqrt(2)),20); E=(20(1+sqrt(2)),0); F=(20,0); G=(0,20); H=(0,20(1+sqrt(2))); J=(10(2+sqrt(2)),10(2+sqrt(2))); draw(A--B); draw(B--C); draw(C--D); draw(D--E); draw(E--F); draw(F--G); draw(G--H); draw(H--A); dot(A); dot(B); dot(C); dot(D); dot(E); dot(F); dot(G); dot(H); dot(J); label("A",A,NNW); label("B",B,NNE); label("C",C,ENE); label("D",D,ESE); label("E",E,SSE); label("F",F,SSW); label("G",G,WSW); label("H",H,WNW); label("J",J,SE); [/asy]

Then $4s+j=45$ , so $j$ can be $1$ , $5$ , or $9$ . - $j=1$ : $s=11$ , so we have $2-9$ , $3-8$ , $4-7$ , $5-6$ , which can be distributed out to the pairs of letters in $4!$ ways, and then there are $2$ ways to choose which number is which letter in each pair so $4!\cdot 2^4$ . - $j=5$ : Really the same as above - $s=10$ , you also have $4$ pairs so also $4!\cdot 2^4$ . - $j=9$ : Also the same - $s=9$ , $4$ pairs so $4!\cdot 2^4$ . Together, $3\cdot 4! \cdot 2^4 = \textbf{(C) 1152}$ .

Thus, J can be  $1$ ,  $5$ , or  $9$ . Our first case is when  $J=1$ . We have  $8$  choices to put one of the remaining numbers. There are  $6$  numbers left that are not corresponding with the first number, so we have  $6$  choices of where to insert one of these numbers. stem_md: Ted's grandfather used his treadmill on 3 days this week. He went 2 miles each day. On Monday he jogged at a speed of 5 miles per hour. He walked at the rate of 3 miles per hour on Wednesday and at 4 miles per hour on Friday. If Grandfather had always walked at 4 miles per hour, he would have spent less time on the treadmill. How many minutes less? $\textbf{(A)}\ 1 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 2 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 3 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 4 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 5$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>On Monday he jogged for  $\dfrac25 \cdot 60 = 24$  minutes. On Wednesdayday he walked for  $\dfrac23 \cdot 60 = 40$  minutes, and on Friday he walked for  $\dfrac24 \cdot 60 = 30$  minutes. If he had walked at  $4$  mph the whole time, he would have walked  $\dfrac{2 + 2 + 2}{4} \cdot 60 = 90$  minutes. Therefore, our answer is 
\[ 24 + 40 + 30 - 90 = \boxed{\textbf{(D)} \ 4}\]</details>

stem_md: What is the ratio of the least common multiple of 180 and 594 to the greatest common factor of 180 and 594? $\textbf{(A)}\ 110 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 165 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 330 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 625 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 660$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Notice  $180 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$  and  $594 = 2 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 11$ . Their greatest common factor is  $2 \cdot 3^2 = 18$  and their least common multiple is  $2^2 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 5 \cdot 11$ , so our answer is  $\dfrac{2^2 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 5 \cdot 11}{2 \cdot 3^2} = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 11 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)} \ 330}$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2013 Contests/2013 AMC 8/564475.json

To find  $\gcd(180,594)$ , we use the euclidean algorithm. We have \begin{align*}
594-3\cdot 180=54 
180-3\cdot 54=18 
54-3\cdot 18=0

So  $\gcd(180,594)=18$ . 

Now we know that \[\gcd(180,594)\cdot lcm(180,594)=180\cdot 594.\] so  $lcm(180,594)=10\cdot 594=5940$ . 

The answer is  $\frac{5940}{18}=\frac{1980}{6}=\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 330}$ .

Just noticed this thread getting a lot of new replies :p I'm going to go ahead and explain my thought process, since apparently seventh-grade me didn't take the time to do so here :)
Here is the solution that you were most likely expecting: We know that two minutes and 45 seconds is 165 seconds. 16.5*6=99, which is very close to 100, so the most likely answer is 100. However, when I took the test, I found a different solution: B. 80 My thought process follows: I first came to the original solution of 99. However, as is the case in many competition math problems you must consider the question of which way to round. For general math, 99 is closest to 100, so 100 would be correct. However, this sparked another point: What would happen at a real railroad crossing? We know 6 cars ENTER in 10 seconds so 99 cars can ENTER in two minutes and 45 seconds. Since the train goes at a constant rate, there can't be any more than 99 cars entering, so there actually can't be a hundred cars in the train! The question is not "Which is closest to the number of cars?" but "Which is the most likely number of cars?" This means that anything 100 and up has a 0% chance of occurring, so C, D, and E are incorrect. We know now that the answer is either A or B. However, we know that 99 cars enter the crossing! What happened? Train crossings take time to cross. This means that 80 cars can enter the crossing and then take time to cross. Then, the gates fall after a total of two minutes and 45 seconds. This would, however, be quite a long crossing. Sure, we could say that such a long crossing could happen. However, here's the other possibility. Trey sees 6 cars in 10 seconds. However, seeing a car does not necessarily mean seeing the whole car. He could see five full cars and half the sixth, but he still sees enough of the sixth car to know that there is a sixth car. Then, the crossing is slightly shorter. This is another possibility for why there could be fewer cars. Now, we have shown that there is a possibility that only 80 cars could enter. However, is it more likely than 60? Yes, I believe so. If we see six full cars in ten seconds, we would have a cross time of about 30 seconds. This gets even shorter as we see less of the sixth car. If we (hypothetically) see five cars and the tiniest sliver of a sixth car possible, so small that it is insignificant in calculations, we would need two minutes to get all the cars into sight and a 45 second crossing. 80 cars have a maximum of a 30 second crossing while 60 have a minimum of 45 seconds during the crossing. This means that 80 cars is a much more likely possibility. With all of this evidence, I believe that the correct answer is B, 80. The answer cannot be C, D, or E since there is a maximum of 99 cars if the crossing takes 0 seconds, so those answers have a 0% chance of occurring, and thus cannot be correct. The answer wants the odds of getting the exact number of cars, not an amount in the range. From there, the crossing of 60 cars is not at all realistic at 45 seconds or more. We thus are left with 80 as the last possibility standing. Thus, I believe that the true answer to this question is B.
The tl;dr is that when trains take time to cross a railroad crossing, 99 cars entering is not the same as 99 cars completing the crossing, and that the six cars did not necessarily fully enter. I sent this off to the MAA and was shot down, with the following two reasons: #1, anything more than "99 cars enter, so clearly 100 is the closest" is overthinking it, especially considering that this is an AMC 8 problem. While I agree that it was pretty silly to put B when I actually took the test, since I actually did have some points to bring up that proved my answer to be correct, the correct answer to the problem should still change. #2, the cars were not necessarily of uniform length. This point, in my view, does have significant merit. However, it was still a matter of determining which is the most likely. Given all the information provided here and assuming that we don't have access to data on whether the front cars of most trains are the largest, this only pushes B and C into being equally likely options. Of course, the key reason that this complaint couldn't have been accepted is that I WAS overthinking it, and this simply isn't what they look for on the AMC 8. If B were an accepted answer, the vast majority of the people who selected it most likely wouldn't have actually thought about the problem to this extent. They informed me that I was the only one to make a complaint of this sort, so if anyone else had a similar thought process to this, they didn't tell MAA about it. Thus, re-scoring would mean giving points to everyone who chose B just because one person could think of a good reason B would be correct (when, I would assume, most people who chose B just got the question wrong and agreed with the solution when it was posted). Although I still feel that B is a legitimate answer, I do understand the MAA's decision, as from the perspective of the contest it would not be feasible to make any change as a result of this complaint. I was overthinking it, and probably should've picked C on the test - I just feel that when going from a perspective of the mathematically correct answer, B is a bit more likely. :)

stem_md: A  $1\times 2$  rectangle is inscribed in a semicircle with longer side on the diameter. What is the area of the semicircle? $\textbf{(A)}\ \frac\pi2 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ \frac{2\pi}3 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ \pi \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ \frac{4\pi}3 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ \frac{5\pi}3$
solution_md: <details><summary>Sol</summary>If we take a quarter-circle from that semi-circle we see that the diagonal of the 1x1 square in that quarter-circle is the radius of the quarter circle, meaning that the radius of the quarter circle is  $\sqrt2$ . This means that the radius of the semi-circle is also  $\sqrt2$  and that means the area of the semi-circle is  $\frac{\pi r^2}2 = \frac{\pi \sqrt2^2}2 = \frac{2\pi}2 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ \pi}.~\blacksquare$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2013 Contests/2013 AMC 8/564490.json

stem_md: A number of students from Fibonacci Middle School are taking part in a community service project. The ratio of  $8^\text{th}$ -graders to  $6^\text{th}$ -graders is  $5:3$ , and the the ratio of  $8^\text{th}$ -graders to  $7^\text{th}$ -graders is  $8:5$ . What is the smallest number of students that could be participating in the project? $\textbf{(A)}\ 16 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 40 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 55 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 79 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 89$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>The ratio of  $8^{\text{th}}$ -graders to  $6^{\text{th}}$  graders is  $5:3 = 40:24$ , and the ratio of  $8^{\text{th}}$ -graders to  $7^{\text{th}}$  graders is  $8:5 = 40:25$ . Therefore, the ratio of  $8^{\text{th}}$  graders to  $7^{\text{th}}$  graders to  $6^{\text{th}}$  graders $ is $ 40: 25: 24 $, resulting in a smallest minimum of $ 40 + 25 + 24 = \boxed{\textbf{(E)} \ 89} $ because $ \gcd(40, 25, 24) = 1$.</details>

stem_md: Abe holds 1 green and 1 red jelly bean in his hand. Bea holds 1 green, 1 yellow, and 2 red jelly beans in her hand. Each randomly picks a jelly bean to show the other. What is the probability that the colors match? $\textbf{(A)}\ \frac14 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ \frac13 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ \frac38 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ \frac12 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ \frac23$
solution_md:
Abe holds 1 green and 1 red jelly bean in his hand. Bea holds 1 green, 1 yellow, and 2 red jelly beans in her hand. Each randomly picks a jelly bean to show the other. What is the probability that the colors match? $\textbf{(A)}\ \frac14 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ \frac13 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ \frac38 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ \frac12 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ \frac23$
SolutionIf Abe picks the green bean, the probability Bea does the same is $\dfrac14$ . If he picks the red bean, the probability Bea does the same is $\dfrac24 = \dfrac12$ . Therefore, our answer is $\dfrac12 \cdot \dfrac14 + \dfrac12 \cdot \dfrac12 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)} \ \dfrac38}$

stem_md: When Clara totaled her scores, she inadvertently reversed the units digit and the tens digit of one score. By which of the following might her incorrect sum have differed from the correct one? $\textbf{(A)}\ 45 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 46 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 47 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 48 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 49$
solution_md:
@Both solution postersYou cannot assume that her score is only two digits.
SolutionLet her original score be $100A+10a+b$ , where $A$ is the number comprised of the digits before the tens and units digits. When she reverses the tens and units digits, her score becomes $100A+10b+a$ . Subtracting these numbers from each other yields $10(a-b) + (b-a)$ , or $9(a-b)$ . Hence, the difference must be a multiple of 9, and the only answer choice that is is $\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 45}$ .

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be an acute triangle with altitudes  $AD$ ,  $BE$ , and  $CF$ , and let  $O$  be the center of its circumcircle.  Show that the segments  $OA$ ,  $OF$ ,  $OB$ ,  $OD$ ,  $OC$ ,  $OE$  dissect the triangle  $ABC$  into three pairs of triangles that have equal areas.
solution_md:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with altitudes $AD$ , $BE$ , and $CF$ , and let $O$ be the center of its circumcircle. Show that the segments $OA$ , $OF$ , $OB$ , $OD$ , $OC$ , $OE$ dissect the triangle $ABC$ into three pairs of triangles that have equal areas. *APMO 2013, Problem 1*
Consider barycentric coordinates with reference triangle $ABC$ . We'll show that the areas of $AOE$ and $BDO$ equal by showing that the ratio of the areas of $AOE$ and $ABC$ is symmetric in $a$ and $b$ . Then we have \begin{align} A&=(1,0,0) B&=(0,1,0) E&=(S_{BC}:0:S_{AB}) \text{ because } AE \text{ is a cevian that passes through }H O&=(a^2S_A:b^2S_B:c^2S_C) \end{align} Now \begin{align*} \frac{[AOE]}{[ABC]}&=\frac{1}{(\sum {a^2S_A})\cdot (S_{BC}+S_{AB})}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 a^2S_A & b^2S_B & c^2S_C S_{BC} & 0 & S_{AB}\end{vmatrix} &=\frac{1}{(\sum {a^2S_A})\cdot (S_{BC}+S_{AB})}(b^2S_B^2S_A) &=\frac{b^2S_{AB}}{(\sum {a^2S_A})\cdot (S_{C}+S_{A})} \end{align*} We can now remove the sum and $S_{AB}$ because both are symmetric in $a$ and $b$ , so it suffices to have $ \frac{b^2}{(S_{C}+S_{A})} $ symmetric but this is trivial since this is equal to $\frac{b^2}{b^2}=1$ , hence we are done. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Determine all positive integers  $n$  for which  $\dfrac{n^2+1}{[\sqrt{n}]^2+2}$  is an integer.  Here  $[r]$  denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to  $r$ .
solution_md:
Let  $n=a^2+b$ , where  $0 \leq b \leq 2a$ . Then  $a^2+2$  must divide
\[a^4+2a^2b+b^2+1 \implies 2a^2b-2a^2+b^2+1 \implies b^2-4b+5.\]

Due to our bound on  $b$ , we require  $\frac{b^2-4b+5}{a^2+2} \in \{1,2,3\}$ , which gives the solutions
\[b = \sqrt{2a^2+3}+2, \quad \sqrt{3a^2+5}+2.\]

Testing modulo 3, neither solutions are integers, giving us  $\boxed{\text{no solutions}}$ .  $\blacksquare$

If $k$ is odd then $k^2+2$ is $3$ mod $4$ but since $(l+2)^2+1$ has no divisor of the form $4k+3$ this gives a contradiction. So let $l=2m$ . Thus $4m^2+2|(l+2)^2+1$ . We first let  $n=a^2+b$ , where  $0 \leq b \leq 2a$ . Then, we need:  $$ \frac{(a^2+b)^2+1}{a^2+2}=a^2+2(b-1)+\frac{(b-2)^2+1}{a^2+2} $$  to be an integer. This is equivalent to saying  $\tfrac{(b-2)^2+1}{a^2+2}$  is an integer, call this  $k$ . We now consider the following cases on which integer  $k$  is:**Case 1:**  $k=1$ . Then we need  $(b-2)^2=a^2+1$ . However, the only consecutive perfect squares are  $0,1$ , which implies  $(b-2)^2=1$  and  $a=0$ . But since  $0 \leq b \leq 2a$ , we also need  $b=0$  which is a contradiction.**Case 2:**  $k=2$ . Then we need  $(b-2)^2=2a^2+3$ . Now take  $\pmod{3}$ , which shows that the LHS is either  $0,1$  and the RHS is either  $0,2$ . This implies that  $b \equiv 2 \pmod{1}$  and  $a \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ , so  $a=3m$  and  $b=3n+2$  for some positive integers  $m,n$ . When we substitute, the equation becomes:  $$ 9n^2=18m^2+3 $$  wherupon taking  $\pmod{9}$  implies that no solutions exist.**Case 3:**  $k=3$ . Then we need  $(b-2)^2+1=3a^2+6$ . Taking  $\pmod{3}$ , the LHS is either  $1,2$  and the RHS is  $0$ , so no solutions exist in this case.**Case 4:**  $k \geq 4$ . This implies  $(b-2)^2+1=ka^2+2k$ . But for  $a \geq 2$  we have:
\begin{align*}
(b-2)^2+1&\geq (2a-2)^2+1
&\geq (2a)^2+1
&\geq 4a^2+1
&\geq ka^2+1
&> ka^2+2k
\end{align*}
so equality never holds (the reason we need  $a \geq 2$  is because the first inequality is not true if  $a=1$  and  $b=0$ , for instance). If  $a=1$  the LHS is still less than the RHS, since the LHS is at most  $2^2+1=5$  and the RHS is at least  $12$ . Thus there are no solutions in this case either.
Combining these cases finishes.  $\blacksquare$

Let  $n=k^2+m$ , where  $k,m$  are both nonnegative integers and  $m \in [0,2k]$ . 

We have that  $\frac{{(k^2+m)}^2+1}{k^2+2} = k^2+2m-2+\frac{m^2-4m+5}{k^2+2}$  needs to be an integer, so  $\frac{m^2-4m+5}{k^2+2}$  needs to be an integer. Since  $m \in [0,2k]$ , we have that  $\frac{m^2-4m+5}{k^2+2}$  can only be  $1,2,$  or  $3$ . I claim that it can't be any. 

If the quantity is equal to  $1$ , we have that  ${(m-2)}^2 = k^2+1$ , and this clearly holds false. 

If the quantity equals to  $2$ , we have that  ${(m-2)}^2=2k^2+3$ . Observing this in mod  $3$ , we see that  $m \equiv 2 \mod 3$  and  $k \equiv 0 \mod 3$ . Let  $m=3m'+2$  and  $k=3k'$ . Substituting these values in we get that  $3{(m')}^2=6{(k')}^2+1$ , which clearly isn't possible again by observing in modulo  $3$ . 

If the quantity is equal to  $3$ , we have that  ${(m-2)}^2=3k^2+5$ . The right hand side is equal to  $2 \mod 3$ , hence this is absurd.

For  $2k$  real numbers  $a_1, a_2, ..., a_k$ ,  $b_1, b_2, ..., b_k$  define a sequence of numbers  $X_n$  by \[
X_n = \sum_{i=1}^k [a_in + b_i] \quad (n=1,2,...).
\] If the sequence  $X_N$  forms an arithmetic progression, show that  $\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^k a_i$  must be an integer.  Here  $[r]$  denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to  $r$ .
solution_md: Take any  $i$  . We have :   $$ \frac{ [a_in+b_i]-b_i+1}{n} \geq a_i \geq \frac{ [a_in+b_i]-b_i}{n} $$   .Summing over from  $i=1 \text{ to } k$  we have ,   $$ \frac{X_n - B_k+k}{n} \geq A_k \geq \frac{X_n - B_k}{n} $$   . Here ,  $B_k= \sum_{i=1 }^k b_i$  and  $A_k= \sum_{i=1 }^k a_i$  . Now from the fact that the  $X_i 's$  are in A.P with integral common difference  $d$  . , it boils down to   $$  \frac{t}{n} + \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot d \geq A_k \geq  \frac{t-k}{n} + \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot d  $$  . Letting  $n \rightarrow \infty$  yields  $A_k=d \in \mathbb{Z}$  as desired . $ \text{Q.E.D.} \blacksquare$ .

Let  $a$  and  $b$  be positive integers, and let  $A$  and  $B$  be finite sets of integers satisfying
(i)  $A$  and  $B$  are disjoint;
(ii) if an integer  $i$  belongs to either to  $A$  or to  $B$ , then either  $i+a$  belongs to  $A$  or  $i-b$  belongs to  $B$ .
Prove that  $a\left\lvert A \right\rvert = b \left\lvert B \right\rvert$ .  (Here  $\left\lvert X \right\rvert$  denotes the number of elements in the set  $X$ .)
solution_md: Define sets $X,Y$ as follows \[X=\{i:i\in A\cup B,i+a\in A\}\] \[Y=\{i:i\in A\cup B,i-b\in B\}\] Note that $X\cup Y=A\cup B$ . Also, the set $X+a=\{i:i=x+a,x\in X\}$ is a subset of $A$ . Similarly the set $Y-b$ is a subset of $B$ . Hence, $|X|\leq|A|$ and $|Y|\leq|B|$ , so $|X|+|Y|\leq|A|+|B|$ . \[|A|+|B|\geq|X|+|Y|=|X\cup Y|+|X\cap Y|=|A\cup B|+|X\cap Y|\]\[=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|+|X\cap Y|=|A|+|B|+|X\cap Y|\geq |A|+|B|,\] so equality must hold. Hence, $|X|=|A|,|Y|=|B|$ and $X\cap Y=\phi$ . It follows that for each $i$ , either $i+a\in A$ , or $i-b\in B$ , both cannot hold simultaneously. Consider the function $f:A\cup B\rightarrow A\cup B$ such that if $x+a\in A$ then $f(x)=x+a$ and if $x-b\in B$ then $f(x)=x-b$ . Claim: This function is injective. Proof. Note that if $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ and $x_1,x_2\in A$ then $x_1=x_2$ is forced. Similarly, if $x_1,x_2,\in B$ then $x_1=x_2$ is forced as well. However, if $x_1\in A$ and $x_2\in B$ , then $x_1+a\in A$ and $x_2-b\in B$ , but since $x_1+a=x_2-b$ , this element lies in both $A$ and $B$ , which contradicts the fact that $A\cap B=\phi$ . So, the function is injective. Since there are exactly $|A|+|B|$ inputs and at most $|A|+|B|$ outputs with each input corresponding to a unique output, it follows that the function is surjective. It is hence bijective. Consider a directed graph $G$ on $|A|+|B|$ vertices where each vertex represents an element of set $A$ or set $B$ . A directed edge $x\rightarrow y$ exists if and only if $y=f(x)$ . Since $a\ne0$ and $b\ne0$ , there are no loops, and the function is bijective, the graph is composed entirely of pairwise disjoint directed cycles, with each vertex being a part of a cycle. Consider a cycle $\mathcal{C}$ of length $l$ consisting of $x_1$ elements from set $X$ and $y_1$ elements from set $Y$ . Then, there are exactly $x_1$ elements from set $A$ and $y_1$ elements from set $B$ in this cycle. Moreover, we return to the original element after $x_1+y_1$ length walk around the cycle. So, if $e$ is our original element, then $e+x_1a-y_1b=e$ . So, $x_1a=y_1b$ . Summing up this equation over all the cycles in graph $G$ , we get $a|A|=b|B|$ , as required. $\blacksquare$

solutionConsider a digraph where where we have $i\to i+a$ (resp. $i\to i-b$ ).**Claim:** The graph is a union of cycles $C_1,C_2,\dots,C_m$ **Proof:** As the graph is finite, we must have sequences of the form $i_1\to i _2\to\dots \to i_n\to \cdots$ , where $i_n$ is the first vertex that has already occurred before, say as $i_k$ . FTSOC if $i_1\to i_2\to \cdots \to i_n\to \cdots$ is not a cycle and finite, then $i_n-a$ has occurred before both $i_n$ and $i_k$ (if $i_n\in A$ ) or $i_n+b$ has occurred before both $i_n$ and $i_k$ (if $i_n\in B$ ). Both cases contradict the minimality assumption. Therefore $i_n=i_1$ and we have a cycle. $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** $C_1, C_2, \dots,C_n$ are disjoint**Proof:** Suppose FTOSC that there exist two cycles $C_i, C_j$ that are not disjoint and $C_i\neq C_j$ . Let $i_s\to \cdots \to i_r$ be the sequence of vertices that is contained in both cycles and consider $i_r$ . But then $i_r \to i_{r+1}'$ in cycle $C_i$ and $i_r\to i_{r+1}''$ in cycle $C_j$ . If $i_{r+1}'\neq i_{r+1}''$ , then the outdegree of $i_r$ is $2$ , a contradiction! So $i_{r+1}'=i_{r+1}''$ , but this contradicts that $i_r$ is the last vertex of the sequence contained in both cycles. Therefore $C_i=C_j$ , but we assumed $C_i\neq C_j$ , so we obtain that all cycles are disjoint. $\blacksquare$ Choose a cycle $C_k=\{i_1,i_2,\dots,i_m\}$ and pick a particular vertex, say $i_s$ . As this is a cycle, we have $i_s=i_s+ax -by$ , where $x,y$ is the number of times we perform $i\to i+a$ and $i\to i-b$ respectively. Therefore $ax=by$ and we note that $x=l_k\frac{\text{lcm}(a,b)}{a}, y=l_k\frac{\text{lcm}(a,b)}{b}, \quad l_k\in \mathbb{Z}^+$ , i.e. $ax=by=l_k\cdot\text{lcm(a,b)}$ are multiples of the $\text{lcm}$ . Using this and claim 2, it follows that \begin{align*}\left(\sum_{i=1}^ml_i\right)\cdot \text{lcm}(a,b)&=a\left(\frac{\text{lcm}(a,b)}{a}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^ml_i\right)&=a|A|&=b|B|&=b\left(\frac{\text{lcm}(a,b)}{b}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^ml_i\right)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^ml_i\right)\cdot \text{lcm}(a,b) \, .\end{align*} This concludes the problem. $\square$

stem_md: Let  $ABCD$  be a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle  $\omega$ , and let  $P$  be a point on the extension of  $AC$  such that  $PB$  and  $PD$  are tangent to  $\omega$ .  The tangent at  $C$  intersects  $PD$  at  $Q$  and the line  $AD$  at  $R$ .  Let  $E$  be the second point of intersection between  $AQ$  and  $\omega$ . Prove that  $B$ ,  $E$ ,  $R$  are collinear.
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>We use Barycentrics on  $\triangle ABC.$  Let  $P=(u:0:v)$  with  $u+v=b.$  Since  $P$  lies on the tangent to  $(ABC)$  at  $B,$  it lies on the line  $a^2z+c^2x=0.$  Thus,  $a^2v+c^2u=0,$  or  $v=-\frac{c^2}{a^2}u,$  or  $P=(a^2:0:-c^2).$ Notice that  $\overline{CP}$  is the  $C$ -symmedian of  $\triangle CBD.$  Hence, by lemma 4.26 of EGMO,  $\overline{BD}$  is the  $B$ -symmedian of  $\triangle ABC.$  Thus,  $D=(a^2:t:c^2).$  But  $D$  also lies on  $(ABC),$  so   $$ a^2tc^2+b^2a^2c^2+c^2a^2t=0, $$   or  $t=-\frac{b^2}{2}.$  Thus,  $D=(a^2:-\tfrac{b^2}{2}:c^2)=(2a^2:-b^2:2c^2).$ We know line  $DP$  is of the form   $$ u_1x+v_1y+w_1z=0, $$   where  $u_1,v_1,$  and  $w_1$  are constants. From  $D,$  we know   $$ 2a^2u_1-b^2v_1+2c^2w_1=0, $$   and from  $P$  we know  $a^2u_1-c^2w_1=0.$  Hence,  $w_1=\frac{a^2}{c^2}u_1$  and   $$ v_1=\frac{2a^2u_1+2c^2\cdot\frac{a^2}{c^2}u_1}{b^2}=\frac{4a^2u_1}{b^2}. $$   Therefore, line  $DP$  has the equation  $x+\frac{4a^2}{b^2}y+\frac{a^2}{c^2}z=0,$  or   $$ b^2c^2x+4a^2c^2y+a^2b^2z=0. $$  Let  $Q=(x_1:y_1:z_1),$  and since  $Q$  lies on the tangent at  $C$  and line  $DP,$    $a^2y_1+b^2x_1=0$  and   $$ b^2c^2x_1+4a^2c^2y_1+a^2b^2z_1=0. $$   Thus  $y_1=-\frac{b^2}{a^2}x_1,$  and substituting gives   $$ b^2c^2x_1-4b^2c^2x_1+a^2b^2z_1=0, $$   or  $z_1=\frac{3c^2}{a^2}x_1.$  Thus,  $Q=(1:-\tfrac{b^2}{a^2}:\tfrac{3c^2}{a^2})=(a^2:-b^2:3c^2).$ We know  $E$  lies on  $\overline{AQ},$  so  $E=(t_1:-b^2:3c^2).$  It also lies on  $(ABC)$  so   $$ a^2(-b^2)(3c^2)+b^2(t_1)(3c^2)+c^2(-b^2)(t_1)=0, $$   or   $$ t_1=\frac{a^2b^23c^2}{2b^2c^2}=\frac{3a^2}{2}. $$   Thus,  $E=(3a^2:-2b^2:6c^2).$ The equation of line  $AD$  is  $u_2x+v_2y+w_2z=0,$  where  $u_2,v_2,$  and  $w_2$  are constants. From  $A,$  we know  $u_2=0.$  From  $D,$  we have  $(-b^2)v_2+(2c^2)w_2=0,$  or  $w_2=\frac{b^2}{2c^2}v_2.$  Hence, the equation of  $AD$  is  $y+\frac{b^2}{2c^2}z=0$  or  $2c^2y+b^2z=0.$ We know  $R=(a^2:-b^2:t_2)$  as  $R$  is on line  $CQ.$  But  $R$  is also on line  $AD,$  so  $-b^2(2c^2)+b^2t_2,$  or  $t_2=2c^2.$ Thus  $[BER]$  is a multiple of \begin{align*}\begin{vmatrix}0&1&03a^2&-2b^2&6c^2 a^2&-b^2&2c^2\end{vmatrix}&=3a^2\begin{vmatrix}-b&2c^21&0\end{vmatrix}+a^2\begin{vmatrix}1&0-2b^2&6c^2\end{vmatrix}&=3a^2(-2c^2)+a^2(6c^2)&=0,\end{align*} so  $B,E,$  and  $R$  are collinear.  $\square$</details>

If you are projecting from a conic $\omega$ to *itself*, then you can project through points not on $\omega$ (and actually projecting through a point on $\omega$ would not make sense in this case). The $B$ -exincircle $w_b$ is tangent to $BA$ and $BC$ in $M$ and $N$ respectively. Denote the projection $K$ of $C$ on $MN$ and the projection $L$ of $C$ on $PQ$ . Prove that $MKLP$ is cyclically. **Proof.** Denote $S\in KM\cap LP$ . Observe that $AM=BP=s-c$ , $MP=a+b$ and $\left\{\begin{array}{c} m\left(\widehat{PMS}\right)=90^{\circ}-\frac B2 m\left(\widehat{MPS}\right)=90^{\circ}-\frac A2 m\left(\widehat{MSP}\right)=90^{\circ}-\frac C2\end{array}\right\|$ . Apply the theorem of **Sines** in $\triangle MPS\ :\ \frac {a+b}{\cos\frac C2}=$ $\frac {SM}{\cos \frac A2}=\frac {SP}{\cos \frac B2}\implies$ $SM^2-SP^2=\frac {(a+b)^2}{\cos^2\frac C2}\cdot\left(\cos ^2\frac A2-\cos^2\frac B2\right)=$ $\frac {ab(a+b)^2}{2s(s-c)}\cdot(\cos A-\cos B)=$ $\frac {ab(a+b)^2}{2s(s-c)}\cdot\frac {2(b-a)s(s-c)}{abc}\implies$ $\boxed{SM^2-SP^2=\frac {(a+b)(b^2-a^2)}{c}}$ . Apply the theorem of **Cosines** in the triangles $CAM$ and $CBM\ :\ \left\{\begin{array}{c} CM^2=(s-c)^2+b^2+2b(s-c)\cos A CP^2=(s-c)^2+a^2+2a(s-c)\cos B\end{array}\right\|\implies$ $CM^2-CP^2=b^2-a^2+2(s-c)(b\cos A-a\cos B)$ . Observe that $b\cos A-a\cos B=$ $\frac {b^2-a^2}{c}$ and $CM^2-CP^2=$ $b^2-a^2+2(s-c)\cdot \frac {b^2-a^2}{c}=\left(b^2-a^2\right)\cdot\left(1+\frac {a+b-c}{c}\right)\implies$ $\boxed{CM^2-CP^2=\frac {(a+b)(b^2-a^2)}{c}}$ . In conclusion, $SM^2-SP^2=CM^2-CP^2=\frac {(b-a)(a+b)^2}{c}\implies$ $SC\perp AB$ . Denote $R\in SC\cap AB$ . Since $RMKC$ and $RPLC$ are cyclically obtain that $\left\{\begin{array}{c} SC\cdot SR=SK\cdot SM SC\cdot SR=SL\cdot SP\end{array}\right\|\implies$ $SK\cdot SM=SL\cdot SP\implies$ $MKLP$ is cyclically.

I post a more general problem (the crux of this one) and some more properties of this configuration.

Consider triangle  $ABC$  and let  $\omega_b,\omega_c$  be the excircles opposite vertices  $B,C$ . Let these touch the sides  $BC,CA,AB$  at points  $B_c,B_b,B_a$  and  $C_b,C_a,C_c$  respectively. Let  $\ell$  denote the exterior angle bisector of  $\angle BAC$  and  $I_b,I_c$  be the centres of these excircles. Let  $X=B_aB_c \cap C_aC_b$  and  $Y=B_bB_c \cap C_bC_c$  and  $M=C_aC_b \cap B_bB_c$  and  $N=B_aB_c \cap C_bC_c$ . Then we make the following observations:

1.) Points  $A,X,Y$  are collinear with  $XY \perp BC$ .
2.)  $MN=\ell$ Proof:- 
We consider the following Lemma:

"There exists a conic  $\mathcal{H}$  which passes through all six points  $B_x,C_y$  with  $x,y \in \{a,b,c\}$ "

Proof of the Lemma is as follows: We fix the points  $B_a,C_a,B_c,C_b$  and prove that the corresponding Ray's subtend the same cross ratio on  $B_b,C_c$ . This is quite simple to compute:  $C_c(B_a,C_b;C_a,B_c)=(B,C_b;C_cC_a \cap BC,B_c)=\frac{a(2a+b+c)}{(b+c-a)^2}$  which is symmetric in  $b,c$  and so these two cross ratios are equal. Therefore, by the projective definition of a conic, we get the validity of our Lemma.

For part 1, we apply Pascal's theorem on the sextuple  $(B_a,B_c,B_b,C_a,C_b,C_c)$  which lies on  $\mathcal{H}$  to get that points  $A,X,Y$  are collinear. Now, some angle chasing gives that  $X$  is the orthocenter of triangle  $YB_cC_b$  (by showing it lies on the other two altitudes) we get that  $XY \perp BC$ .

For part 2, we apply Pascal's theorem on the sextuple  $(B_a,B_c,B_b,C_c,C_b,C_a)$  which lies on  $\mathcal{H}$  to get that points  $M,N,B_bC_c \cap B_a,C_a=T$  are collinear. Notice that it is clear that  $MN \parallel \ell$  by simple angle chasing. Now, we have  $B_b,B_a$  are symmetric in  $\ell$  and  $C_cC_a$  are also symmetric in  $\ell$  and therefore,  $T \in \ell$  meaning that  $MN=\ell$ .

Use standard triangle notation for  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ ,  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$ , and  $s$ . By a well-known fact,  $MB = MN = AP = AQ = s$ .

Let  $\ell_A$  and  $\ell_A'$  be the perpendicular bisectors of  $PQ$  and  $PL$ , respectively. Then lines  $\ell_A$  and  $\ell_A'$  are parallel, and the distance between them is  $d_A = \tfrac{QL}2$ . Also, since  $APQ$  is isoceles with vertex  $A$ , line  $\ell_A$  bisects  $\angle PAQ$ .

Let  $\ell_B$  and  $\ell_B'$  be the perpendicular bisectors of  $MN$  and  $MK$ , respectively. Then lines  $\ell_B$  and  $\ell_B'$  are parallel, and the distance between them is  $d_B = \tfrac{NK}2$ . Also, since  $BMN$  is isoceles with vertex  $B$ , line  $\ell_B$  bisects  $\angle MBN$ .

Thus, the four lines  $\ell_A$ ,  $\ell_A'$ ,  $\ell_B$ ,  $\ell_B'$  form a parallelogram  $IXYZ$ , where  $I = \ell_A \cap \ell_B$  is the incenter of  $\triangle ABC$ ,  $X = \ell_A' \cap \ell_B$ ,  $Y = \ell_A' \cap \ell_B'$ , and  $Z = \ell_A \cap \ell_B'$ . Let  $I'$ ,  $X'$ ,  $Y'$ , and  $Z'$  be the projections of  $I$ ,  $X$ ,  $Y$ , and  $Z$ , respectively, onto line  $AB$ . We claim that  $Y'$  is the midpoint of  $AB$ .

We compute  $I'X'$ . Note that the acute angle between  $\ell_B$  and line  $AB$  is  $\tfrac{B}{2}$ , so  $I'X' = IX \cos \tfrac{B}{2}$ . Also note that, by a well-known fact,  $\angle AIB = 90 + \tfrac{C}{2}$ , so  $I'X' = IX \cos \tfrac{B}{2} = d_A \cos \tfrac{B}{2}/\cos \tfrac{C}{2}$ . Now  $d_A = \tfrac{QL}{2} = \tfrac{QC}{2} \sin \tfrac{A}{2} = \tfrac{(s-b)}{2} \sin \tfrac{A}{2}$  since  $QC = QA - AC = s - b$ , so \[I'X' = \frac{s-b}{2} \sin \frac A2 \cdot \frac{\cos \tfrac B2}{\cos \tfrac C2}.\] Now we make some propositions, which can be verified easily using the half-angle formulas and the Law of Cosines: \[\sin \frac A2 = \sqrt{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}}, \quad \cos \frac B2 = \sqrt{\frac{s(s-b)}{ac}}, \quad \cos \frac C2 = \sqrt{\frac{s(s-c)}{ab}}.\] These formulas give \[I'X' = \frac{s-b}{2} \cdot  \sqrt{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{s(s-b)}{ac}} \div \sqrt{\frac{s(s-c)}{ab}} = \frac{(s-b)^2}{2c}.\] By symmetry, we can write  $I'Z' = \frac{(s-a)^2}{2c}$ , which also equals  $X'Y'$  since  $IXYZ$  is a parallelogram. Thus, noting the well-known fact  $AI' = s-a$ , we have \[AY' = AI' + I'X' - X'Y' = (s-a) + \frac{(s-b)^2}{2c} - \frac{(s-a)^2}{2c}\] and substituting  $s = \tfrac{a+b+c}{2}$ , this simplifies to just  $AY' = \tfrac c2 = \tfrac{AB}{2}$ . Thus,  $Y'$  is indeed the midpoint of  $AB$ . Since  $MB = AP$ , we see that  $Y'$  is also the midpoint of  $MP$ . Thus,  $YY'$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $MP$ , so the perpendicular bisectors of  $MK$ ,  $PL$ , and  $MP$  are concurrent, at  $Y$ . Thus, quadrilateral  $MKLP$  is cyclic.</details>

<details><summary>Motivation</summary>The solution looks intimidating at first, but the idea behind it is actually pretty natural: if we can prove that the perpendicular bisectors of a quadrilateral concur, then the quadrilateral is cyclic. The perpendicular bisector of  $MP$  is really just the perpendicular bisector of  $AB$ , since  $AM = BP$ . We notice that the perpendicular bisector of  $MK$  is parallel to that of  $MN$ , which is just the  $A$ -bisector of  $\triangle ABC$  since  $MAN$  is isosceles with vertex  $A$ . stem_md:
Determine all positive integers  $x$ ,  $y$  and  $z$  such that  $x^5 + 4^y = 2013^z$ .

(*Serbia*)
solution_md: First we start with a claim - Key observation is that $2013= 3.11.61$ **Claim - ** $5 \mid y$ Proof - For this note that $x^{5} \equiv -4^{y} \mod 11$ and $$ -4^{y} \equiv 7 , 6 , 2 , 8, 10 \mod 11 $$ and as $$ x^{5} \equiv 1 , -1 \mod 11 $$ , so only thing common in both residues is $-1$ , giving $5 \mid y$ . Now let $y = 5k$ , so we can rewrite the equation as $x^5 + 4^{5k} = 2013^z$ , so any prime dividing $x + 4^k$ must be from the set ${3, 11, 61}$ , also if $p \mid x + 4^k$ , then $\nu_p({x + 4^k}) = z$ (say from LTE) as $gcd(5 , 3.11.61) = 1$ , so if $2$ primes divide $x + 4^k$ , then we get $$ x + 4^k \ge 3^{z}. 11^{z} $$ , but from Power mean inequality we have $$ \frac{x^5 + 4^{5k}}{2} \ge \frac{(x^5 + 4^k)^5}{32} \longrightarrow 2013^z \ge \frac{33^{5z}}{16} $$ which obviously causes size issues. So $x + 4^k = p^z$ where $p \in {3, 11, 61}$ , but note that again from Power Mean Inequality , we get that $$ 3^z . 61^z . 11^z \ge \frac{p^{5z}}{16} $$ , which gives $p = 3$ , but this fails as this gives(from Binomial Theorem) $$ (x+4^k)^5 > x^5 + 4^{5k} = 3^z . 61^z . 11^z > 3^{6z} = (x+4^{k})^6 $$ , a contradiction. Hence we have no solutions. $\blacksquare$

Now let  $B=4^a$ . Then  $2013^z = x^5 + 4^{5a} = (x+B)(x^4 - x^3B + x^2B^2 - xB^3 + B^4)$ . Observe that the factors on the right are coprime - as if  $p$  is a common prime divisor of both, then  $B\equiv -x \pmod p$  and the second factor gives  $5x^4 \equiv 0 \pmod p$ ; however  $p$  divides  $2013$ , so  $p$  cannot be  $2$  or  $5$  and so  $p\mid x$ , whence  $p\mid B = 4^a$ , contradiction! 

Having in mind  $2\leq x+B < x^4 - x^3B + x^2B^2 - xB^3 + B^4$  for except for  $x=B=1$  (to prove that, check quickly  $x=B$  and now without loss of generality let  $x>B$  - then the inequality is equivalent to  $x^3(x-B) + x(B^2(x-B)-1) + B^4 - B > 0$  which is true), we deduce that  $x+B = 3^z$  or  $x+B = 11^z$  or  $x+B = 33^z$ . If  $x+B \geq 11^z$ , then by the Power-Mean inequality we have  $2013^z = x^5 + B^5 \geq \frac{(x+B)^5}{16} \geq \frac{11^{5z}}{16}$ , contradiction; while if  $x+B = 3^z$ , then  $2013^z = x^5 + B^5 < (x+B)^5 = 243^z$ , contradiction. Therefore there are no solutions.

stem_md:
Let  $S$  be the set of positive real numbers. Find all functions  $f\colon S^3 \to S$  such that, for all positive real numbers  $x$ ,  $y$ ,  $z$  and  $k$ , the following three conditions are satisfied:

(a)  $xf(x,y,z) = zf(z,y,x)$ ,

(b)  $f(x, ky, k^2z) = kf(x,y,z)$ ,

(c)  $f(1, k, k+1) = k+1$ .

(*United Kingdom*)
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The answer is   $$ f(x, y, z) = \boxed{\frac{y+\sqrt{y^2+4xz}}{2x}} $$   only. This can be easily seen to satisfy  $(a), (b)$ , and  $(c)$ . Now, we show that it is the only solution. Let  $f(x, y, z) = zg(x, y, z)$ . Then, we have that   $$ g(x, y, z) = g(z, y, x), $$     $$ kg(x, ky, k^2z) = g(x, y,z), $$   and   $$ g(1, k, k+1) = 1. $$   By the first and second properties, we can deduce that
\begin{align*}
g(x, y, z) &= kg(x, ky, k^2z) 
           &= kg(k^2z, ky, x) 
           &= kg((k^2z),\frac{1}{k}(k^2y), \frac{1}{k^2}(k^2x)) 
           &= k^2g(k^2z, k^2y, k^2x) 
           &= k^2g(k^2x, k^2y, k^2z). 
\end{align*}   
Since  $k^2$  can reach every positive real as  $k$  varies on positive reals, we have that   $$ g(x, y, z) = \frac{1}{x}g\left(1, \frac{y}{x}, \frac{z}{x}\right). $$   Now, I claim that   $$ g(1, r, s) = \frac{r+\sqrt{r^2+4s}}{2s}. $$   To show this, note that if  $k = \frac{r+\sqrt{r^2+4s}}{2s}$ , then  $k^2s-kr = 1$ , and since  $k > 0$ , we have by the second property that   $$ g(1, r, s) = kg(1, kr, k^2s) = k = \frac{r+\sqrt{r^2+4s}}{2s}, $$   where the last step is by the third property. So the claim is true. Thus, it follows that 
\begin{align*}
g(x, y, z) &= \frac{1}{x}g\left(1, \frac{y}{x}, \frac{z}{x}\right) 
           &= \frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{\frac{y}{x} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2 + 4\frac{z}{x}}}{2\frac{z}{x}}\right) 
           &= \frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{y+\sqrt{y^2+4xz}}{2z}\right) 
           &= \frac{y+\sqrt{y^2+4xz}}{2xz}.
\end{align*}
Thus,   $$ f(x, y, z) = zg(x, y, z) = \frac{y+\sqrt{y^2+4xz}}{2x}, $$   as claimed.  $\blacksquare$</details>

In a mathematical competition, some competitors are friends; friendship is mutual, that is, when  $A$  is a friend of  $B$ , then  $B$  is also a friend of  $A$ . 
We say that  $n \geq 3$  different competitors  $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$  form a *weakly-friendly cycle*if  $A_i$  is not a friend of  $A_{i+1}$  for  $1 \leq i \leq n$  (where  $A_{n+1} = A_1$ ), and there are no other pairs of non-friends among the components of the cycle.

The following property is satisfied:

"for every competitor  $C$  and every weakly-friendly cycle  $\mathcal{S}$  of competitors not including  $C$ , the set of competitors  $D$  in  $\mathcal{S}$  which are not friends of  $C$  has at most one element"

Prove that all competitors of this mathematical competition can be arranged into three rooms, such that every two competitors in the same room are friends.

(*Serbia*)
solution_md:
$\mathfrak{The \;Twenty-Second\; Of\; August,\; 2025}$ ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ Beautiful problem! The solution I managed to find it quite long, here is a rough sketch to it.
Solution - grinding Graph Theory$$ \color{red} \spadesuit\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Rough sketch.}}\color{red} \spadesuit $$ We solve the following problem, equivalent to the one stated above:
Let $G$ be a graph with the property that for any chordless cycle $C$ and any vertex $v$ not in $C$ , at most one vertex of $C$ is adjacent to $v$ . Prove that $G$ is three-colorable. (A chordless cycle is a cycle where no two vertices are adjacent unless they are consecutive in the cycle.)
Without loss of generality, we consider connected graphs; it can easily be seen how this solution can be generalized for disconnected graphs. We proceed by induction on the number of cycles in our graph. The base case is clear - simply consider a tree and color the root red, all vertices directly connected to the root blue, all connected to them red again etc. Now, suppose this was a spanning tree of the graph we are considering, and suppose we wanted to add cycles to our graph. It can easily be seen that the chordless condition is equivalent to connecting two leaves with an edge (of course, for every time that there is a cycle) such that no leaf is connected like this more than once. Thus, we can simply paint one of these leaves in the third color, say, green, and we are done.
